findings.title: Case-sensitive exact-match lookup lets blocked users bypass the block by changing email case
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, a case-sensitive exact string match (Postgres `=` is case sensitive by default), and the model's `uniqueness: true` validation on `email` is likewise case-sensitive. Since nothing normalizes/downcases the email before storing a BlockedEmail row or before looking it up, an admin blocking `spammer@example.com` will fail to catch the exact same address submitted as `Spammer@Example.com` or `SPAMMER@EXAMPLE.COM`. This defeats the entire purpose of the feature with a trivial, common bypass (most mail providers treat the local part/domain case-insensitively).

findings.title: Validator persists DB writes as a side effect, and is invoked twice (or more) per signup, inflating block statistics
findings.body: `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, which increments `match_count` and sets `last_match_at` and saves the row every time it's called. Validations are not guaranteed to run only once: in `UsersController#create` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb) `user.valid?` is called explicitly and then `user.save` runs validations again internally, so for a single signup attempt against a blocked email the counters get incremented twice. Additionally, any other code path that calls `user.valid?` without actually persisting the user (e.g. checks, previews, specs) will silently write to the `blocked_emails` table and skew `match_count`/`last_match_at`, even though no real signup attempt occurred. Validators should not have unconditional persistent side effects like this.

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write race on match_count
findings.body: `should_block?` reads `record.match_count`, increments it in Ruby, then calls `record.save`. Concurrent requests that match the same blocked email (a realistic scenario for automated spam signups hitting the same address) can read the same starting value and overwrite each other's increments, silently losing count updates (classic lost-update race). This should use an atomic SQL increment (e.g. `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", ...)` or `increment_counter`) instead of read-then-save.

findings.title: No tests added for new `errors`/`values` response fields or blocked-email rejection flow
findings.body: The `create` action now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` on failed signup, which the JS controller depends on to populate `rejectedEmails`. No controller/request spec is added or updated to verify this new response shape, nor is there an integration test exercising the end-to-end scenario of signing up with a blocked email and getting the expected error payload. This is a meaningful behavior/contract change with no regression coverage.

findings.title: Whitelist/blacklist domain validation logic moved out of User but has no test coverage in the new spec
findings.body: The domain-restriction logic (`email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist`) was moved from `User#email_validator` into `EmailValidator`, but `email_validator_spec.rb` only exercises the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch (lines 9-21). There is no test in this new spec verifying the whitelist/blacklist behavior that was relocated, so a regression in that moved logic (e.g. wrong attribute/value being validated) could go unnoticed if the previous coverage (if any) wasn't preserved elsewhere.

findings.title: rejectedEmails default array literal is a shared prototype property across controller instances
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined as a plain array literal directly on the `Ember.Controller.extend()` definition rather than created per-instance (e.g. via `init()` or a computed property). In Ember's object model, array/object literal defaults declared this way are shared across all instances of the class unless explicitly reset in `init`. If more than one instance of `CreateAccountController` is ever created (e.g., in tests, or if the controller is not a true singleton), mutations via `pushObject` will leak between instances/sessions, causing stale 'rejected' emails to persist incorrectly across unrelated signup attempts.
